segments.title: Bounding the Royal Navy's 1900 research counterfactual
segments.body: The premise gives the Royal Navy a blank cheque for research from 1900. Early changes would accumulate, so extending the exercise to the present would require assumption after assumption. The period therefore has to remain limited enough for plausible alternatives to be traced. The question is how greater funding changes development within those limits.

evidence.note: The premise is a Royal Navy blank cheque for research from 1900, bounded to a manageable historical period.

segments.summary: The scenario gives the Royal Navy research funding from 1900 while limiting how far its accumulating consequences can be projected.

segments.title: Why government money changes naval innovation
segments.body: Government funding changes the risk a firm has to carry. Earlier naval research was largely financed by manufacturers, with governments often arriving at procurement or offering facilities for trials. A commercial firm needs a likely return and risks bankruptcy if an ambitious project fails. Improving a 12-inch gun into a 13.5- or 14-inch weapon is consequently a safer proposition than jumping straight to 18 inches. A public research fund can absorb failures that private investors would reject, including work that only becomes useful through a later adaptation. The counterfactual moves some of that risk onto the Admiralty so builders can advance more quickly.

evidence.note: Commercial exposure to failed projects favours incremental development, while public funding can absorb more ambitious research risks.

segments.summary: Government funding can support high-risk naval experiments that private firms would normally pursue only in smaller, safer steps.

segments.title: Exploration, proven routes and commercial investment
segments.body: The East India Company analogy separates the initial exploration of a route from the later business of exploiting it. In this comparison, governments finance exploratory voyages and bear the risk of finding nothing useful. Once a route and its destination are known, a company can estimate potential returns and raise money to operate along it. The same reasoning explains why a navy might pay for an unproved technology before a manufacturer can justify selling it.

evidence.note: The East India Company comparison distinguishes government-backed exploration from commercial investment after a route has been proved.

segments.summary: The East India Company comparison separates the risk of exploring a route from the later commercial work of operating along it.

segments.title: Could Dreadnought have gas turbines by 1904?
segments.body: The suggested 1904 date would allow only four years from the start of the research programme. That is too short for the proposed gas-turbine leap. The counterfactual has to remain within the period's practical development possibilities.

evidence.note: A suggestion of gas turbines for Dreadnought by 1904 rejected as an implausibly rapid development from a 1900 start.

segments.summary: A four-year research programme beginning in 1900 cannot deliver the suggested gas-turbine Dreadnought.
segments.question: Could research funding from 1900 put gas turbines into Dreadnought by 1904?
segments.answerShort: No. That timetable asks too much of the available technology and the British development system, even with additional funding.

segments.title: The industrial scale behind Edwardian naval innovation
segments.body: The largest Edwardian armament companies could supply a country's railways, military equipment and civil engineering through one commercial relationship. Vickers and Armstrong Whitworth belonged to an industrial world in which a single salesman could arrange far more than weapons alone. Britain had roughly four or five firms on this scale, depending on the period and definition, the largest concentration of such commercial power in the comparison. Smaller shipyards could be capable builders without matching that breadth. A naval research programme would therefore have access to established firms with extensive manufacturing resources and customers.

evidence.note: Major Edwardian armament firms could supply ships, guns, railways, ports, and army equipment through one relationship, a much broader range than less integrated modern contractors offer.

segments.summary: Vickers, Armstrong Whitworth, and comparable firms could supply whole national military systems, giving Britain unusual leverage over naval innovation.

segments.title: Quantity and quality in Edwardian naval competition
segments.body: The Anglo-German naval race centred on the number of ships each side could deploy. Germany's drive for a fleet too large for Britain to fight was particularly threatening because it sat just across the North Sea, and Germany had traditionally been Britain's landward partner. Britain, the United States, Italy and Japan also competed over the quality and prestige of individual ships. A competitor could answer a single superior battleship with a later design, while several second-best ships still gave their owner substantial military power. Germany had the industry to join this qualitative competition, but its navy lacked the political weight to fund both races alongside the army. The scenario therefore has to consider how a British research programme changes foreign spending and industrial priorities.

evidence.note: The threat of German fleet numbers across the North Sea, international competition over individual ship quality, and the German Navy's funding rivalry with the Army.

segments.summary: The threatening Anglo-German contest over fleet numbers differed from a looser international competition to build the most impressive individual ship.

segments.title: British turbines spread through sales and licences
segments.body: British firms supplied turbines to all four powers competing over ship quality at some points in this period. Britain also sold Parsons turbines to Germany during their numerical naval race. A typical path was to buy complete British units, purchase a licence, and then use that knowledge to expand domestic production. Brown-Curtis and other turbine programmes meant the technology would not remain a permanent British monopoly. Admiralty-funded acceleration could strengthen Britain's export industry while also helping rival navies close the gap.

evidence.note: British firms supplied turbines to the powers competing over ship quality and to Germany, with foreign buyers following imports by licensing production.

segments.summary: Britain sold Parsons turbines even to Germany, while foreign buyers often followed imports with licensed domestic production.

segments.title: Buying time through parallel machinery trials
segments.body: Capital ships demand proven machinery because a major breakdown becomes a strategic and political embarrassment. Turbinia had demonstrated a working steam turbine in 1897, eight years before Dreadnought, so the difficulty was proving it at capital-ship scale. German buyers were also willing to purchase Parsons turbines while their own machinery was still being developed because reliability mattered more than the supplier's nationality. Without computer simulation, builders had to construct engines and run them ashore to accumulate operating experience. A private company could limit its exposure by testing one expensive engine over a long period. Admiralty funding could support several engines running simultaneously and produce the required evidence much sooner.

evidence.note: Capital-ship machinery required proven reliability, and parallel engine trials could accumulate the necessary operating experience sooner.

segments.summary: Funding several engines at once can accumulate operating hours faster than a builder testing a single expensive prototype.

segments.title: Jellicoe's boiler decision and the cost of proving machinery
segments.body: Small-tube boilers were technically possible when Jellicoe considered machinery for the Queen Elizabeth class, but they had not accumulated enough testing to be judged viable. As Third Sea Lord, he could ask what machinery was ready but lacked discretionary money to commission the missing trials. The counterfactual gives him the option of paying for a batch of boilers and demanding results within the design timetable. An illustrative schedule allows two months to build them and another two months to test them, making a decision after four months conceivable. A private firm would be more likely to run a few boilers over a longer period because it would carry the loss if the trials failed.

evidence.note: Jellicoe's lack of discretionary testing funds and an illustrative four-month programme to build and run enough boilers for a timely decision.

segments.summary: Discretionary funding could let Jellicoe commission the missing small-tube boiler trials before the Queen Elizabeth machinery decision.

segments.title: Hull experiments need a customer willing to pay
segments.body: Model basins normally tested hulls for funded construction projects, which left little commercial reason to pursue an unrelated design idea. Additional research money could support comparisons before a specific ship order justified them. Dr Clarke recalls friends testing the hull shown on screen and finding it economical at about 24 knots, although it had been intended for a 21-knot ship. Hull design also has to balance a stable firing platform in calm weather with acceptable motion and stability in rough seas. Royal Navy armoured cruisers show how useful hull lines developed through two or three generations of refinement.

evidence.note: Model-basin funding, hull stability and a recalled test of the unidentified on-screen hull.

segments.summary: Model-basin and hull work normally follows funded ship projects, but a research budget could support more deliberate testing of speed and seakeeping.

segments.title: Engine endurance tests behind maintenance intervals
segments.body: Modern maintenance intervals also depend on evidence about how engines behave over long periods. The illustrative example specifies three engines running for 250,000 hours each, alongside continuous maintenance and recorded results. Computer calculations and fatigue averages can supplement practical running tests. Test engines may be connected to the electricity grid so their output is useful during endurance work.

evidence.note: An illustrative three-engine endurance test, fatigue calculations, and use of test-engine output for electricity generation.

segments.summary: Long maintenance intervals require endurance evidence, supported by fatigue calculations and practical tests whose output can supply the electricity grid.

segments.title: Testing 14-inch guns and triple turrets earlier
segments.body: Gun development requires firing, fatigue testing, and sometimes destructive trials, all of which become faster when several barrels are available. Government money could fund six or nine barrels from the outset, compared with the one to three a firm might risk itself. Governments usually helped fund a second batch after company testing, but earlier support could use the manufacturing already being set up for the first batch. Elswick had a 14-inch 45-calibre proposal, while Vickers had triple-turret concepts that British yards had not yet been paid to prove. A three-gun turret could fire a ranging salvo without relying on another heavy turret. Funding would make existing proposals testable and establish whether the guns and mountings were suitable for service.

evidence.note: Parallel barrel trials could accelerate Elswick's proposed 14-inch gun, while a three-gun turret could fire a ranging salvo without relying on another heavy turret.

segments.summary: The Admiralty could accelerate proposed 14-inch guns and triple turrets by funding more barrels, proof trials, and mounting work from the outset.

segments.title: Do gun trials come before turret trials?
segments.body: Barrels are usually tested mainly in open mounts at first. Turret trials follow as a separate programme, and some mountings are proved before installation aboard ships. Turrets can subsequently remain at shore firing ranges for testing later gun barrels and production batches.

evidence.note: Gun barrels normally start in open-mount trials, with separate turret proving and continued use of some mountings at shore ranges.

segments.summary: Barrels can be proved in open mounts while the complete turret follows its own testing programme.
segments.question: Are naval guns normally tested in open mounts before turrets are proved?
segments.answerShort: Usually yes: gun testing precedes a separate turret-testing programme, although installed turrets can later support continuing barrel trials.

segments.title: Armour weight, stability and independent shell trials
segments.body: Navies specify armour by weight over an area, such as pounds per square foot, because its weight and position affect the ship's stability. Thickness is an easier way for a general audience to picture the plate. Denser, better armour takes up less space, while its placement affects the centre of gravity and metacentric height. Manufacturers resist paying for trials that cost money and could expose faults in their own armour. A separate Admiralty research budget would let the Navy conduct firing tests with its own guns and plates. Earlier testing could improve shell performance, armour quality and ship design before the First World War.

evidence.note: Armour procurement by weight per unit area, its effect on stability, and independent Navy funding for shell and plate trials.

segments.summary: Navies design armour around weight and protection, while independent shell-and-plate trials could expose problems before a war tests them.

segments.title: Jellicoe's tenure and demands for armour testing
segments.body: Jellicoe's place among the Lords of the Admiralty at Edward VII's funeral in May 1910 is offered as evidence that he remained Third Sea Lord. On that reading, he probably continued until the next appointment in December. His demands for more shell and armour testing would therefore not establish that he was removed early. Reginald Bacon is treated as assisting in the office, with his forthcoming move to Coventry Ordnance Works as further context.

evidence.note: Interpretation of Jellicoe's funeral role and tenure, rejecting an early removal attributed to demands for shell and armour testing.

segments.summary: Jellicoe's place at Edward VII's funeral is used to question the idea that demands for stricter trials forced him out of office early.

segments.title: A workable 1900 Admiralty research system
segments.body: A modern DARPA-style agency depends on a network of universities and research institutes that does not fit the setting of Edwardian Britain. The proposed alternative combines an Admiralty staff reform with discretionary funds for the Sea Lords. The First Sea Lord would gain support for operations and strategy, while the Second and Third Sea Lords could sponsor work within their existing responsibilities. A staff could retain experience between appointments and moderate the effects of sharply different personalities. Its members would also be influenced by a long-serving First Sea Lord, carrying some of that influence into the next administration. The research programme therefore depends on changes to authority and continuity as well as additional money.

evidence.note: Constraints on copying modern DARPA and the proposed combination of Admiralty staffs, discretionary funds and continuity between appointments.

segments.summary: The scenario expands Third Sea Lord funds and gives the First Sea Lord a staff able to preserve continuity between appointments.

segments.title: Arthur Wilson and the railway question his office could not answer
segments.body: The proposed British plan was to land the Army on Germany's Baltic coast, but Army planners asked how quickly strategic railways could move German troops against the landing. Wilson answered that he did not know, an honest response that left the naval case politically exposed. The suggested reply Fisher might have given was that German forces would be committed against France or Russia, so even threatening a Baltic landing could force a diversion. The episode shows why successful fleet command did not by itself equip a First Sea Lord for inter-service and ministerial debate. Staff reform would connect intelligence, strategy, logistics, and political preparation instead of leaving the service's plan in one officer's head.

evidence.note: Wilson's answer to a question about German railway mobilisation and the contrast between his unsupported First Sea Lord's office and his earlier Third Sea Lord's staff.

segments.summary: An Army question about German railways exposes why the First Sea Lord needed staff support for intelligence, joint planning, and political argument.

segments.title: Why the First Sea Lord lacked a formal staff
segments.body: The Admiralty already contained specialist intelligence, logistics, procurement, training, and civil-service organisations, but the First Sea Lord lacked an equivalent operational staff. That gap reflected a Victorian image of the self-sufficient Age of Sail admiral who supposedly issued complex plans through personal genius. The image wrote wives and daughters out of the story even though women aboard ships often performed informal clerical and coordinating work. Senior officers also claimed that keeping war plans in one admiral's head reduced the danger of espionage. Keeping plans unwritten meant they could be lost if something happened to the admiral. The proposed staff reform would trade that supposed secrecy for written plans, institutional memory, political preparation, and continuity between successive Sea Lords.

evidence.note: Existing Admiralty departments, the First Sea Lord's lack of operational staff, informal clerical work by naval women, and objections to writing down war plans.

segments.summary: Victorian ideals of individual admiralship and fear of leaking written plans obscured the staff work that officers, civil servants, and naval families already performed.

segments.title: Could a new First Sea Lord replace the inherited staff?
segments.body: An incoming admiral could not dismiss officers from the service simply because he disliked them. Replacing an inherited staff required finding other postings for its members, appointing replacements and maintaining the work of the office throughout. That made an immediate wholesale change impractical. William May's ability to work under both Kerr and Fisher also shows how senior officers could bridge rival camps. Factionalism could still damage individual careers, but it did not divide every capable officer into an irreconcilable faction.

evidence.note: Staff replacement required alternative postings and continuity of service, while May worked successfully under both Kerr and Fisher.

segments.summary: Personnel rules and officers able to work across factions would help an Admiralty staff preserve continuity between successive First Sea Lords.
segments.question: Could a new First Sea Lord immediately replace the staff inherited from his predecessor?
segments.answerShort: Wholesale replacement would take time because officers needed other postings, replacements had to be found, and the office still had to function.

segments.title: How discretionary funds would work inside the Admiralty
segments.body: The proposed reform would strengthen the other members of the Admiralty Board while giving the First Sea Lord a staff of his own. The Second Sea Lord could seek discretionary funds for accommodation and facilities at training establishments. The Third Sea Lord could approach the Treasury directly for research and development projects, while the First Sea Lord could seek money for large exercises, fuel or particular operational needs. Each would report progress to the Board. The Controller would still shape procurement by selecting the options presented for approval and then managing the chosen work. A strong First Sea Lord could continue to exercise considerable influence, so this arrangement would moderate personal power without eliminating it.

evidence.note: Separate discretionary funds for training facilities, technical development and operational work, with reporting to the Admiralty Board.

segments.summary: The counterfactual gives each Sea Lord funds suited to his responsibilities, with direct Treasury access and continued accountability to the Admiralty Board.

segments.title: Does a Sea Lord have to be a peer?
segments.body: Holding a Sea Lord's office does not require a peerage. The office title alone does not mean its holder is a lord.

evidence.note: A direct clarification that a Sea Lord need not be a lord.

segments.summary: A Sea Lord's office does not require its holder to be a peer.
segments.question: Does a Sea Lord have to be a peer?
segments.answerShort: No. Holding a Sea Lord's office does not require a peerage.

segments.title: Arthur Wilson's likely technical priorities
segments.body: Wilson's experience with battleships, HMS Vernon and the experimental torpedo squadron makes guns, turrets and torpedoes plausible priorities for his research budget. His industrial connections suggest a route to funding Elswick's 14-inch 45-calibre gun. His preference for a high volume of heavy fire also supports trials of Vickers triple turrets. On a pre-dreadnought, a three-gun turret at each end could fire its own ranging salvo. Earlier work on 21-inch torpedoes could strengthen destroyer armament, while the 18-inch weapons mentioned alongside them were intended for submarines. Funding begun in 1900 would not put the 14-inch gun into service by 1902, though development could be underway when Wilson left office. The proposed change funds technology once a company knows it can build it, before the company has paid to prove that it works.

evidence.note: Wilson's experience and industrial contacts, proposed gun and turret trials, larger destroyer torpedoes, and the distinction between starting development and fielding a weapon.

segments.summary: Wilson's experience with battleships, torpedoes, and experimental work makes heavy guns, triple turrets, and larger torpedoes plausible early projects.

segments.title: Arthur Wilson wins the Victoria Cross at El Teb
segments.body: At the Battle of El Teb on 29 February 1884, a lieutenant attached to the Naval Brigade's right half-battery was mortally wounded. Captain Arthur Wilson of HMS Hecla took the officer's place rather than send another subordinate forward. When attackers charged the detachment, Wilson fought in front of sailors who were still harnessed to and hauling their gun. He held the position until soldiers of the York and Lancaster Regiment reached them. The accounts cited describe him fighting eight men with a sword, apparently killing about four and being wounded before assistance arrived. The action earned Wilson the Victoria Cross and supplies useful context for the unusually hands-on officer later entrusted with naval procurement.

evidence.note: At El Teb, Wilson took over a Naval Brigade gun detachment, defended its crew, and received the Victoria Cross.

segments.summary: Before becoming a procurement leader, Wilson took over a Naval Brigade gun detachment at El Teb and protected its crew until infantry support arrived.

segments.title: William May's fast, distributed fleet
segments.body: May wanted dispersed cruising groups whose commanders could conduct their own operations and use radio to coordinate with the rest of the fleet. They would concentrate when an enemy force required it, then separate again for other missions. He exercised the Atlantic and Home Fleets along those lines and later used Dreadnought as his flagship. Speed addressed a central objection to dispersed forces: an enemy might concentrate first and defeat the groups separately. May pushed for Dreadnought to make 21 knots, and the scenario gives him reason to fund better boilers and continue the 14-inch gun programme. Crystal detectors and valve reception systems also offered projects through which his contacts could improve wireless communication. His political connections would help protect this work, as illustrated by the government's reluctance to risk his resignation over further cuts to naval estimates.

evidence.note: May's dispersed cruising groups, fleet exercises, demand for speed, political influence, and proposed boiler, gun and wireless projects.

segments.summary: May's preference for fast, coordinated cruising groups directs the hypothetical budget toward machinery, heavy guns, and wireless communication.

segments.title: When did Yarrow start developing small-tube boilers?
segments.body: Yarrow began developing small-tube boilers in 1877 and fitted one to a torpedo boat in 1887, after ten years of development. Thornycroft provided another early example in HMS Daring in 1893. By the period of this counterfactual, more efficient boilers existed but needed further testing before adoption in battleships. Additional funding could accelerate that testing and support May's demand for faster ships. The boilers available through early investment would still differ from designs developed twenty years later.

evidence.note: Yarrow's development began in 1877 and produced an installation in 1887, followed by Thornycroft and the testing needed for battleships.

segments.summary: Yarrow's ten-year path from development to a torpedo-boat installation shows why promising boilers still needed funding and trials before battleship use.
segments.question: When did Yarrow start developing small-tube boilers?
segments.answerShort: In 1877. Yarrow fitted one to a torpedo boat in 1887 after ten years of development.

segments.title: What a 24-knot Dreadnought might look like
segments.body: The working design combines a 24-knot speed with twelve 14-inch guns, making that performance the new battleship baseline in this scenario. Earlier experiments on armoured cruisers could establish superfiring arrangements before their adoption in Dreadnought. Six-inch secondary guns would engage cruisers trying to constrain her speed while leaving the heavy guns available for enemy capital ships. A numerous three-inch battery would deal with destroyers and torpedo boats. Turreted secondary guns follow the Lord Nelson approach of improving firing arcs over casemates. Twin six-inch mountings are preferred because crews handling the guns manually could obstruct one another in a cramped triple wing turret. An alternative with a fifth triple 14-inch turret would lengthen the hull and might reach about 26 knots, although that remains a more ambitious possibility than the working design.

evidence.note: The proposed twelve-gun, 24-knot Dreadnought, earlier superfiring trials, separate anti-cruiser and anti-torpedo batteries, and the space and hull-length consequences of alternative turret arrangements.

segments.summary: The conservative sketch is a 24-knot Dreadnought with twelve 14-inch guns, six-inch cruiser defence, and abundant light guns against torpedo craft.

segments.title: Lord Nelson as the step before the alternative Dreadnought
segments.body: The proposed Lord Nelson would carry triple 14-inch turrets forward and aft alongside 9.2-inch secondary guns. It could also receive small-tube boilers if the early machinery trials succeeded. Its construction and testing would give the Admiralty experience before designing Dreadnought. That experience would join the influence of Tsushima, Cuniberti's ideas, South Carolina and Satsuma. The later ship would therefore build on an altered predecessor as well as on international developments.

evidence.note: Projected Lord Nelson armament and possible boilers, followed by the influences feeding into Dreadnought.

segments.summary: Earlier guns, turrets and boiler trials could first change Lord Nelson, giving the Admiralty a different foundation for Dreadnought.

segments.title: Why a 14-inch 45-calibre gun may beat a longer barrel
segments.body: The Royal Navy's worldwide commitments make barrel endurance more than a workshop issue. Worn barrels in the Far East need replacements shipped out and the old weapons returned to Britain for repair. In this scenario, a 14-inch 45-calibre gun already outranges many prospective rivals, so the extra wear of a 50-calibre design may be a poor bargain. Choosing the larger calibre with a shorter barrel preserves a useful range advantage while reducing how often that global replacement cycle occurs. Against contemporary 11-inch and 12-inch guns, the proposed 14-inch/45 already offers the range advantage being sought.

evidence.note: The preference for 45-calibre barrels links wear and pressure to worldwide replacement logistics, while a 14-inch gun already offers an advantage over prospective opponents.

segments.summary: A larger but shorter-calibre gun can preserve range while reducing barrel wear and the global logistics burden of frequent replacement.

segments.title: Would the gun choice make replacement cranes cheaper?
segments.body: The comparison is between a 12-inch 50-calibre gun and a 14-inch 45-calibre gun. Both require substantial lifting equipment when their barrels are changed. The weight difference is judged too small to make much difference to crane costs, so cheaper lifting equipment does not materially strengthen the case for this gun choice.

evidence.note: The 12-inch/50 and 14-inch/45 comparison gives too little difference in gun weight to produce a substantial saving in replacement cranes.

segments.summary: Both gun options still need heavy cranes, and their weight difference is judged too small to produce a meaningful saving in lifting equipment.
segments.question: Would choosing a 14-inch 45-calibre gun instead of a 12-inch 50-calibre gun reduce the cost of the cranes needed to change it?
segments.answerShort: The difference would be too small to matter much: both weapons still require substantial cranes.

segments.title: Who else could build an early 14-inch naval gun?
segments.body: The United States is the likeliest alternative because Britain and America have industrial organisations large enough to fund and pursue the programme. Germany's Krupp could in theory contribute, but shifting development effort from land weapons would create a difficult argument with the Army. Austria-Hungary's Škoda has the technical capacity, yet lacks the comparable funding and intent. The distinction is between being able to build a gun and having an institution willing to pay for its development.

evidence.note: British and American funding capacity compared with Krupp's competing Army work and Škoda's lack of funding and intent.

segments.summary: Britain and the United States are the powers most able to support an early 14-inch naval-gun programme at the required scale.
segments.question: Could any country besides Britain have developed 14-inch naval guns sooner?
segments.answerShort: The United States is the likeliest rival; other firms had capabilities, but their funding, industrial scale, or political priorities made the programme less viable.

segments.title: Experimental 24-inch torpedoes by 1910
segments.body: Larger torpedoes would be another route by which capital-ship research spread through the fleet. The scenario expects work on experimental 24-inch weapons by 1910. Successive senior officers had come through torpedo and gunnery appointments, giving them a recurring interest in greater range and striking power. Discretionary funds would let them sustain that work across changes of officeholder. This is a projection of development activity, with no claim that a 24-inch torpedo would already be operational.

evidence.note: Projected work on 24-inch torpedoes by 1910 and the recurring influence of officers with torpedo and gunnery backgrounds.

segments.summary: Successive torpedo and gunnery officers could keep funding larger, longer-range torpedoes, reaching experimental 24-inch weapons by 1910.

segments.title: Henry Jackson's wireless and fire-control opportunity
segments.body: Jackson demonstrated ship-to-ship wireless over three miles in 1896 and extended the range to roughly 140 miles within about eighteen months, working with Marconi and shipyards. In an 1899 exercise, wireless-equipped ships let their admiral manoeuvre his force and outmatch an opponent without the same communications. His election to the Royal Society in 1901 also gave him connections among people pursuing scientific and engineering work. His friendship with Percy Scott could link discretionary communications funding to director fire-control trials. Once a device could be built, that funding could support nine or twelve examples instead of three, speeding testing before the system was fully proven. Better radio and director fire control reaching service around 1910 would leave four years for the fleet to adapt before war. Smaller radio sets could also reach torpedo boats and aircraft. Early radar remains a possibility under discussion, but radar-directed gunnery in the First World War is explicitly judged very unlikely.

evidence.note: Jackson's wireless ranges and exercises, scientific connections, larger trial batches, and the distinction between plausible earlier radio and director systems and much less certain radar-directed fire.

segments.summary: Jackson's early wireless work and links to Percy Scott make radio communications and director fire control especially promising targets for accelerated trials.

segments.title: Percy Scott refuses an order that would collide two cruisers
segments.body: During a 1908 Channel Fleet manoeuvre, Charles Beresford signalled two parallel cruiser columns about six cables apart to turn inward together. Percy Scott recognized that the order would put the leading ships, Good Hope and Argyll, on a collision course and directed that it be disobeyed. The decision avoided a disaster comparable to the Camperdown collision, but Beresford sought to have Scott court-martialled. The Admiralty refused, although Scott's sea career was effectively over. In the counterfactual, discretionary research money could instead employ him ashore and fund the director-fire-control work that the service already wanted him to continue.

evidence.note: Scott's refusal of Beresford's inward-turn signal, the threatened collision of Good Hope and Argyll, and the subsequent court-martial dispute and unfunded fire-control work.

segments.summary: Scott disobeyed a 1908 manoeuvring signal that would have turned Good Hope and Argyll into one another, then faced Beresford's demand for a court martial.

segments.title: Jellicoe and the compounding capital-ship race
segments.body: A 24-knot battle line would raise the speed demanded of cruiser attack forces, with about 30 knots proposed for that role. Earlier gun funding could also shift the progression from 14-inch weapons to 15.5-inch or 16-inch guns in Orion equivalents, followed by still larger calibres in the Queen Elizabeth generation. The possible later ships range widely because the next usable gun depends on which development projects succeed. A Queen Elizabeth equivalent might aim for 30 knots and achieve 28, just as the historical design fell short of its intended speed. Funded shell and armour trials could supply Greenboy-equivalent ammunition from the outset, avoiding the need for the later corrective shell programme. A 28-knot ship carrying twelve 18-inch guns is tentatively estimated at 50,000 to 60,000 tons. Britain's 1910 shipyard-upgrade cycle could respond to this growth in requirements. Foreign responses and the results of intermediate trials make a precise third-generation design impossible to predict.

evidence.note: Higher cruiser speeds, successive gun-calibre increases, a possible 28-knot Queen Elizabeth equivalent, earlier shell trials, and shipyard expansion remain conditional on development and foreign responses.

segments.summary: Once the first faster Dreadnought exists, later designs could seek larger guns, faster battlecruisers, better shells, and yard expansions to support them.

segments.title: How large would the projected super-dreadnought be?
segments.body: A ship combining twelve 18-inch guns with 28-knot speed is tentatively estimated at roughly 50,000 to 60,000 tons. That is an estimate for the scenario rather than a completed design. Shipbuilding infrastructure could expand in response to the programme, and Britain's historical 1910 yard upgrades later supported ships as large as Hood. Earlier growth in capital-ship requirements could redirect that investment cycle towards the proposed fleet. A direct comparison with Yamato also needs care because its Second World War requirements included protection against aircraft and extra subdivision.

evidence.note: The tentative displacement estimate, Britain's 1910 yard upgrades and later ability to build Hood, and the different protection requirements of Yamato.

segments.summary: A 28-knot battleship with twelve 18-inch guns might reach 50,000 to 60,000 tons, requiring the shipyard expansion that Britain was already undertaking in 1910.
segments.question: How heavy would a 28-knot battleship armed with twelve 18-inch guns be?
segments.answerShort: Roughly 50,000 to 60,000 tons, with Britain's 1910 shipyard-upgrade cycle expanding the capacity needed to build it.

segments.title: Germany faces an earlier choice between army and navy
segments.body: The scenario makes Nassau look inadequate against a British ship with greater speed, heavier guns, and a much larger broadside. Tirpitz would then face a political conflict over funds with the German Army. Germany could seek more naval money, accept fewer ships to pay for qualitative improvements, pursue an alternative strategy, or reduce naval ambitions. The existing budget could not support both the proposed qualitative competition and the numerical race. An alternative strategy would not automatically mean an immediate turn to U-boats, since French and British submarine investment was ahead at this point. Such a funding dispute could remove Tirpitz and reshape German policy, although that is one possible outcome of the counterfactual.

evidence.note: Nassau's disadvantage against the proposed British ship and the choices between extra funding, reduced numbers, alternative strategies, or lower naval ambitions.

segments.summary: A much faster, better-armed British Dreadnought could make Germany choose between costly qualitative competition, an offset strategy, or reduced naval ambitions.

segments.title: How a German naval retreat could weaken the Entente
segments.body: The Entente Cordiale of 1904 did not remove every source of diplomatic strain. Relations with Russia and later crises still influenced Britain's position. If a serious German naval challenge disappeared and events such as the Moroccan crisis took a different course, the Entente could weaken or fall apart. Under those conditions, and provided Germany avoided Belgium, Britain might remain outside a continental war against the Triple Alliance.

evidence.note: The Entente's continuing strains, relations with Russia, later diplomatic crises, and Belgium qualify the possibility of Britain remaining outside a continental war.

segments.summary: A reduced German naval threat could change Britain's continental commitments, but relations with Russia, later crises, and Belgium remain conditions on that outcome.

segments.title: Italy responds with Mediterranean speed and firepower
segments.body: Italy lacks the resources to compete simultaneously in fleet numbers and individual ship quality, while its production infrastructure better suits the latter. Dante Alighieri's twelve 12-inch guns and 22-knot speed provide the starting point. A response to the proposed British Dreadnought might keep 12-inch guns but increase the battery to six triple turrets, producing an eighteen-gun broadside. Older Italian weapons of 17 inches and 16.25 inches would not supply a ready modern naval gun without substantial further development. Speed would help cover both coasts, with France on one side and Austria-Hungary in the Adriatic on the other. Italian design changes could also affect Russia's Gangut programme because Dante Alighieri is presented as its design basis.

evidence.note: Italy's production limits, a possible eighteen-gun response, older large-calibre weapons, Mediterranean commitments, and the proposed consequences for Gangut.

segments.summary: Italy is likely to answer a British technological lead by pursuing high-quality, fast, heavily armed ships suited to its Mediterranean geography.

segments.title: Could Britain sustain its research lead?
segments.body: Continued naval research could sustain an early British lead if it produced returns for British industry. A fleet that deterred war would also protect the economic base paying for the programme. Whether Britain remained ahead would depend on the money other states committed to their own development. A major war or political interference could alter that balance. The scale of the industrial return and the reactions abroad remain open questions in the scenario.

evidence.note: Research returns for British industry, deterrence, foreign funding, war, and political interference determine whether the early lead lasts.

segments.summary: Britain might preserve an early advantage if research spending generates industrial returns and deters a destructive fleet race, but no permanent lead is guaranteed.
segments.question: Could the Royal Navy stay far enough ahead that no rival could match its pace of development?
segments.answerShort: Possibly for a time, especially if the programme strengthens industry and deters war, but rival funding and politics make a permanent lead impossible to predict.

segments.title: Japan learns by ordering the lead ship abroad
segments.body: Japanese naval development already followed a pattern of buying a sophisticated first example, observing its construction, and applying the knowledge domestically. Earlier battleships and armoured cruisers supplied that experience, while the Kongō programme provides the battlecruiser parallel. In this scenario Japan might order both a lead battlecruiser and a battleship from British yards, then build the rest of their classes at home. Paying for the design and sending Japanese personnel to observe construction would transfer methods as well as drawings. Japan would still assess how many ships its strategy required. A higher British baseline would change the qualities sought in those ships.

evidence.note: Buying a lead ship in Britain to transfer skills and construction knowledge to Japanese yards.

segments.summary: Japan could use British yards for an advanced lead ship, transferring the construction knowledge needed to build follow-on ships at home.

segments.title: The United States answers with turbines, guns, and turrets
segments.body: South Carolina-class ships would look less competitive if British capital ships combined a heavy broadside with high speed. Matching that speed would push the United States toward turbines instead of continuing to compare turbine ships with triple-expansion machinery. The country has the industrial capacity to answer with larger guns, but American practice normally seeks to exceed rather than merely duplicate a British calibre jump. Triple turrets remain a timing problem because the path from the South Carolina programme to a working battleship mounting historically took about six years. A much more heavily armed Dreadnought could therefore provoke an earlier crash programme while still leaving the first American response dependent on what machinery and mountings were actually ready.

evidence.note: American industrial capacity, turbine adoption, gun-calibre competition, and the development time needed for triple turrets.

segments.summary: An advanced British Dreadnought could push the United States toward turbines, larger guns, and an earlier crash programme for triple turrets.

segments.title: Could fifteen 14-inch guns price Germany out of the race?
segments.body: A Dreadnought with fifteen 14-inch guns in five centreline triple turrets would impose a much greater problem than the conservative twelve-gun option. The comparison uses Nassau's eight-gun broadside and a rough equivalence of three 14-inch guns to four 12-inch guns. That illustrates the scale of the proposed gap rather than a precise prediction of battle results. In this scenario Germany would struggle to fund the research and ships needed to preserve numerical competition, forcing a choice between quality and withdrawal. Very large calibres would still face loading and rate-of-fire limits, so the preferred weapon remains the heaviest shell that can sustain a useful battleship firing rate. Fast battleships could also fill the speed requirement behind the first Invincibles, allowing Britain to build an enlarged Dreadnought class instead.

evidence.note: Fifteen-gun Dreadnought option, rough Nassau broadside comparison, firing-rate constraints, and possible replacement of the first Invincibles.

segments.summary: The strongest Dreadnought option would force Germany to fund a much larger technical response and could also replace the first Invincibles in British plans.

segments.title: Would very heavy shells stop the race towards bigger guns?
segments.body: Germany could leave the race in fleet numbers while continuing to compete over the quality of individual ships. Such a contest would reward visible technical achievements and status. Heavy 18-inch shells would make further growth awkward, yet a prestige project might still reach 22-inch guns. That is an extreme possibility for a showpiece, with the rest of a navy's ships remaining more practical.

evidence.note: Heavy 18-inch shells as a practical constraint and a speculative 22-inch prestige weapon.

segments.summary: A competition for prestige could produce oversized showpieces alongside more practical warships.
segments.question: Would the weight of 18-inch shells prevent navies pursuing still larger guns?
segments.answerShort: Heavy shells are a real drawback, but a prestige race could still produce ships with extremely large guns while the rest of the fleet remained more practical.

segments.title: Why battlecruisers carry the guns of their battleship generation
segments.body: British battlecruisers carry the main guns of their battleship generation partly because they are status assets. Their cruiser-killing role alone would not require the proposed jump from 12-inch to 14-inch guns. Both calibres overwhelm the armoured cruisers considered here. Scharnhorst and Gneisenau at the Falklands illustrate how existing 12-inch fire could already destroy those opponents.

evidence.note: Same-generation capital-ship guns as a status choice, with the Falklands showing the existing power of 12-inch guns against armoured cruisers.

segments.summary: The case for 14-inch battlecruiser guns includes status, since 12-inch fire already overwhelms contemporary armoured cruisers.

segments.title: The horizon could push naval spotting forward
segments.body: The horizon limits how far a ship can observe for itself. Longer-range guns could therefore create an earlier requirement for aircraft to spot and report fall of shot. That demand might also bring aircraft carriers forward. Another possibility is a radio system through which destroyers and torpedo boats ahead of the battle line provide spotting reports. These are alternative development paths whose timing remains open.

evidence.note: Horizon limits, possible earlier aircraft spotting, and forward destroyers or torpedo boats reporting by radio.

segments.summary: Guns that reach beyond direct sight could encourage aircraft spotting or radio reports from smaller vessels ahead of the fleet.

segments.title: Austria-Hungary's route to a fast battleship
segments.body: The Tegetthoff class already carried twelve 12-inch guns in triple turrets. In this scenario, an enlarged version with 14-inch guns would build on that arrangement. A comparable Italian programme could encourage Austria-Hungary to push the design further. The historical ships made about 20 knots and did not need especially long range. A more ambitious programme could pursue fast battleships of about 28 knots, although that remains a proposed outcome.

evidence.note: The Tegetthoff arrangement, possible 14-inch guns, Italian competition, and a speculative increase from about 20 to 28 knots.

segments.summary: Austria-Hungary already has a useful triple-turret foundation and could pursue faster, high-quality battleships in response to Italian and British advances.

segments.title: Fast battleships and battlecruisers have different speed jobs
segments.body: The labels describe operational relationships rather than a universal speed threshold. A fast battleship must keep contact with the fleet's cruiser screen so it can support the scouting line in action. A battlecruiser needs enough extra speed to move beyond that screen and conduct independent reconnaissance or interception. British practice used a cruiser-line benchmark near 28 knots, and other navies commonly measured their ships against Royal Navy equivalents. A 24-knot battle line in this scenario could push the cruiser standard towards 30 knots. Queen Elizabeth-class ships might then reach 28 knots if they fell short of that target, or 30 knots if sustained small-tube-boiler work succeeded.

evidence.note: Cruiser-line support and independent reconnaissance as different speed requirements, with a faster battle line raising the scenario's benchmark.

segments.summary: A fast battleship must maintain contact with the cruiser line, while a battlecruiser must outrun that line for independent reconnaissance.

segments.title: A higher Dreadnought baseline reshapes smaller navies
segments.body: The ripple effects extend beyond the major builders because foreign navies often buy from British or American yards and use their ships as benchmarks. France begins from the institutional legacy of the Jeune École, while Russia must rebuild after the Russo-Japanese War and may again draw on Italian design ideas. Brazil and Chile buy in Britain, Argentina buys in the United States, and their regional dreadnought competition would therefore import the higher standard directly. Spain's requirement for a ship able to overmatch any visiting cruiser would also become more expensive as cruisers grow alongside the battle line. The Royal Navy's historically balanced Jutland fleet provides the warning: its cruisers and destroyers were proportioned to the capital force, whereas Germany's pursuit of battleship numbers left too few cruisers and torpedo boats too small for equivalent work. Fleets that cannot afford many capital ships face the hardest choice because each purchase must deter regional rivals without consuming the rest of a balanced fleet.

evidence.note: France, South American orders, Russia, and Spain would all face a changing capital-ship baseline.

segments.summary: If British Dreadnoughts set a much higher standard, France, Russia, Spain, and South American buyers all face a more expensive and unsettled naval market.

segments.title: Would missing oil storage prevent an earlier fuel transition?
segments.body: Storage facilities were built in response to the decision to construct oil-fired battleships. Earlier small-tube boilers could make oil attractive sooner and bring that investment forward. A British lead in oil firing would also affect commercial shipping. After World War I, American oil-powered merchant ships helped challenge British shipping by avoiding dependence on Britain's coaling network. Earlier British investment could prevent that opening or make the competition more contested.

evidence.note: Oil storage follows battleship construction decisions, with consequences for British coaling influence and American merchant competition.

segments.summary: Oil storage followed battleship orders historically, so earlier adoption could bring infrastructure forward and change competition with American merchant shipping.
segments.question: Would the absence of a global oil-storage network prevent Britain adopting oil-fired battleships earlier?
segments.answerShort: The network could be built in response to ship orders, as it was historically; earlier reliable small-tube boilers could create the demand sooner.

segments.title: Where would an earlier oil-fired fleet get fuel?
segments.body: Iran and other sources within the Empire are raised as possible suppliers for an earlier oil-fired fleet. A funded Admiralty requirement could encourage companies to search for and exploit oil. The oil and extraction methods were available before the Queen Elizabeth programme, while storage was built in response to ship orders. Confidence in the boilers and their operational advantages remained the limiting factors. Earlier machinery development could therefore pull the supporting infrastructure forward.

evidence.note: Existing oil and extraction methods, prospective Iranian or imperial supply, and infrastructure built once reliable boilers justify demand.

segments.summary: The oil and extraction technology existed; reliable boilers and sufficient naval demand would bring supply contracts, storage, and distribution forward.
segments.question: Where would Britain obtain and support enough oil for an earlier oil-fired fleet?
segments.answerShort: The oil and extraction methods already existed; a credible naval requirement would encourage companies to secure supplies and build the necessary storage and distribution system.

segments.title: How might the 1910 Town-class cruisers change?
segments.body: The capital-ship research programme would also affect smaller fleet types. Historically mixed four-inch and six-inch batteries might give way to twin open mounts or, if turret work matured, a more concentrated six-inch arrangement. Earlier experiments with secondary turrets and superfiring positions on armoured cruisers or battleships would reduce the risk of adopting them on a Town. One possible arrangement has six 6-inch guns in three twin turrets, two forward and one aft, with twin 4-inch mounts along the hull sides. The exact layout remains uncertain because the programme's intermediate trials would determine what was ready.

evidence.note: Possible twin open mounts or three twin 6-inch turrets, with 4-inch mounts and earlier superfiring experiments.

segments.summary: A higher fleet baseline could give Town-class cruisers twin gun mountings or turrets, especially if earlier capital-ship trials had already proved superfiring layouts.
segments.question: What would the 1910 Town-class cruisers look like in this alternate research programme?
segments.answerShort: They might carry twin open mounts or a turreted six-inch battery, depending on whether earlier secondary-armament and superfiring trials had matured in time.

segments.title: How would Britain defend offshore oil installations?
segments.body: Extracting oil beneath the sea is more complicated than working a land field. Additional funding could advance the work, but its timing would depend on technical breakthroughs. Defence would rely on the fleet and patrol ships stationed near the installations. Hydrophones are suggested as a possible means of warning of an approaching threat.

evidence.note: Offshore extraction is harder than land production, with fleet patrols and possible hydrophones protecting installations.

segments.summary: Earlier offshore extraction would require patrol ships and underwater warning measures, although developing seabed production would remain harder than exploiting land fields.
segments.question: Would earlier North Sea oil development require new Royal Navy bases or forces to protect offshore assets?
segments.answerShort: It would likely require patrol ships and underwater warning around the installations, though offshore extraction itself would be the first major technical hurdle.

segments.title: Why not simply keep the 12-inch gun?
segments.body: The research fund is intended to seek a qualitative edge. The 12-inch gun is already in dependable production and needs less developmental help. Elswick offers a 14-inch proposal, while other firms also consider 13.5-inch and 14-inch designs. The hoped-for precedent is Warrior and Black Prince's effect on competition with France: a leap large enough to discourage the rival from continuing. In this interpretation, Dreadnought's historical advance had been insufficient to produce that effect on Germany. Funding the larger gun offers another chance at the disruptive advantage the Admiralty wants.

evidence.note: Mature 12-inch guns contrasted with Elswick's 14-inch proposal and the desire to repeat the disruptive advantage associated with Warrior.

segments.summary: The proposed research budget targets a larger gun because the 12-inch weapon is already serviceable and the Admiralty wants a decisive qualitative advantage.
segments.question: Why would the Royal Navy fund a 14-inch gun instead of staying with the 12-inch gun already in production?
segments.answerShort: The point of the investment is a qualitative leap: a 14-inch gun offers a meaningful advantage where the 12-inch gun is already mature and serviceable.

segments.title: Could Britain obtain naval oil from Iraq or Canada?
segments.body: Iraq is accepted as a plausible source for the proposed oil-fired fleet. Canada provides another option, so the supply problem does not depend on a single region. Canadian oil supplied Britain during World Wars I and II. That wartime example supports the argument that Britain could seek fuel through several commercial and imperial connections.

evidence.note: Iraq as a possible supplier and Canadian oil supplies to Britain in both world wars.

segments.summary: Iraq is a possible supplier, while Canadian oil offers another source and a wartime precedent.
segments.question: Would Britain look to Iraq for oil?
segments.answerShort: Probably, but Iraq was one option among several, including Canada and its large supplies.

segments.title: Would Britain tolerate German expansion eastward?
segments.body: Withdrawal from the naval race could force Germany to reconsider its strategy. In this scenario Britain would tolerate a German war directed eastward against Russia, given poor Anglo-Russian relations during much of the period. A German advance through France after absorbing a French attack is also treated as less likely to draw Britain in if it avoids Belgium. The Franco-Prussian precedent allows for a limited defeat of France, while taking over France or threatening the Channel would exceed that tolerance. The result depends on Germany's conduct and territorial aims after abandoning the naval challenge.

evidence.note: Conditional British tolerance of German war aims against Russia and France, with Belgium and the Channel affecting the decision.

segments.summary: Without a German naval challenge or an invasion of Belgium, Britain might tolerate a war directed against Russia or a limited defeat of France.
segments.question: If Germany left the naval race, how much eastward or continental expansion would Britain tolerate?
segments.answerShort: Britain might tolerate war against Russia or a limited defeat of France, but an invasion of Belgium or domination of France would be much more likely to trigger intervention.

segments.title: Could firms export government-funded technology?
segments.body: Modern secrecy assumptions do not apply uniformly to Edwardian procurement. Communications technology might receive tighter protection, while a large gun could remain an export product after the Royal Navy secured priority access. A funding agreement could give the government first refusal or a share of revenue from foreign sales. Such terms would let public investment support British industry without surrendering every commercial opportunity. Admiralty funding could therefore coexist with the international arms market described earlier.

evidence.note: Possible first-refusal and export-profit terms for publicly funded weapons, with tighter secrecy around radio technology.

segments.summary: Britain might reserve first refusal, secrecy for sensitive communications, and a share of export profits rather than prohibit every foreign sale.
segments.question: Would the British government allow firms to sell technology developed with public naval funding abroad?
segments.answerShort: Probably under conditions: Britain could keep first refusal, protect especially sensitive systems, and claim a share of export profits rather than impose a blanket ban.

segments.title: Would submarines and anti-submarine warfare advance sooner?
segments.body: The question proposes bringing E-class-like submarine capability forward, but the scenario leaves the design unresolved. Other powers' choices would strongly affect submarine development. Both undersea weapons and anti-submarine warfare would probably receive substantial funding. The timing of a practical depth charge is another open question, so the funding premise alone does not yield a definite earlier submarine or countermeasure.

evidence.note: Early E-class-like submarines remain unpredicted because foreign responses are unresolved, while submarine and ASW funding could also affect depth-charge development.

segments.summary: Submarine outcomes remain open, but both undersea weapons and countermeasures would receive more attention in this research-rich environment.
segments.question: Could submarines comparable to the E class appear earlier in this scenario?
segments.answerShort: Possibly, but the outcome depends heavily on foreign reactions; both submarine development and anti-submarine work would likely receive more funding.

segments.title: What limits the size of a battleship?
segments.body: A battleship of around 120,000 tons is proposed as technically conceivable, without a worked design. The harder question is whether the Royal Navy could afford and sustain enough ships of that size. Its normal commitments from the 1920s onward are estimated here to require roughly 24 battleships available for service, including squadrons for home waters, the Mediterranean, and the East. Each increase in individual ship size must therefore justify its effect on fleet numbers. Operational coverage and support would impose a practical limit before a theoretical maximum displacement did.

evidence.note: A speculative 120,000-ton ship compared with the estimate of 24 available battleships needed for dispersed Royal Navy commitments.

segments.summary: The limiting factor is less a theoretical maximum displacement than the number of ships a global navy needs and can sustain.
segments.question: Is there a practical upper limit to battleship size in this scenario?
segments.answerShort: Very large ships are technically possible, but the practical limit is set by how many ships the Royal Navy needs and can sustain across its commitments.

segments.title: Could aircraft carriers arrive before the First World War?
segments.body: Longer-range guns and director fire control could create an earlier need for aerial spotting. Balloons had already been considered and found of doubtful value, though the scenario allows another attempt before turning to heavier-than-air aircraft. If director firing developed early enough, a carrier could emerge around 1914 or earlier. An unexpected radar breakthrough would alter that incentive, but aircraft are treated as the more realistic path. No fixed carrier design or introduction date follows from the argument.

evidence.note: Demand for aerial spotting, disappointing balloon work, and a possible carrier around 1914 or earlier if director fire control matures soon enough.

segments.summary: Earlier director fire control could create demand for spotting aircraft and a carrier around 1914 or earlier, depending on how the supporting technologies develop.
segments.question: Could aircraft carriers appear before the First World War in this timeline?
segments.answerShort: Possibly: earlier long-range director firing could drive demand for aircraft spotting and a carrier by about 1914 or before, but the result depends on how the technologies develop.

segments.title: Why did this Admiralty reform not happen?
segments.body: The alternative combines contemplated naval-staff ideas with more formal discretionary funding. Establishing a staff could have made the proposed research programme more likely. The relevant reforms were considered but were never implemented. No single person can be assigned responsibility, since the Admiralty consensus and many Sea Lords did not support a staff.

evidence.note: Considered staff reforms remained unimplemented because Admiralty consensus and many Sea Lords opposed a staff.

segments.summary: The proposed reform lacked Admiralty support, so responsibility cannot be assigned to one person.
segments.question: Who prevented this kind of Admiralty research reform from happening?
segments.answerShort: No single person did; the reform was considered but not implemented because Admiralty culture and consensus did not support it strongly enough.

segments.title: Could motor torpedo boats help develop aircraft engines?
segments.body: Lighter and more powerful engines are a prerequisite for useful carrier aircraft. Motor torpedo boats are another likely recipient of the proposed research money. Boats and aircraft often share engines in this period, allowing improvements to move between the two fields. A naval propulsion programme could therefore advance aviation before the Admiralty began building carriers.

evidence.note: Shared motor-torpedo-boat and aircraft engines provide a route towards lighter, more powerful aviation propulsion.

segments.summary: Motor torpedo boats and aircraft share a need for light, powerful engines, so funding one could accelerate the other.
segments.question: Would lighter, more powerful engines have to come before aircraft carriers?
segments.answerShort: Yes, but motor-torpedo-boat research could help because boats and aircraft often shared engines in this period.

segments.title: How early could gas turbines arrive?
segments.body: The gas-turbine timetable depends on which projects receive funding. Earlier support for Whittle provides one possible route to jet-turbine development. Even with that support, the machinery would take time to mature. The scenario leaves the result open and gives no year for a breakthrough.

evidence.note: Possible earlier funding for Whittle, with no firm date for a working gas turbine.

segments.summary: Earlier funding for work such as Whittle's could accelerate gas turbines, although no firm arrival date is proposed.
segments.question: How early might gas turbines emerge in this alternate timeline?
segments.answerShort: Earlier funding for Whittle or comparable work could accelerate development, but a working turbine would still take time and no date can be fixed.

segments.title: Vickers aircraft and long-range gunnery
segments.body: Vickers was already advertising aircraft alongside HMS Princess Royal before World War I. Its range of products gave it an industrial interest in both naval weapons and aviation. Guns able to reach farther would create demand for a way to see the enemy at those distances. A company working in both fields could propose aircraft as part of the solution and put more money into their development.

evidence.note: Vickers' prewar aircraft business and the incentive to supply aerial observation for longer-range naval guns.

segments.summary: Firms already selling both warships and aircraft could pursue aerial spotting to make longer-range guns useful.

segments.title: The 15-inch/42 gun supplies the funding model
segments.body: The counterfactual borrows the funding model used for the 15-inch/42 gun. The same approach is applied to other projects by moving naval support into an earlier stage of development. The test is whether funding an existing proposal sooner could make it ready when a ship programme needed it. This gives the scenario a historical procurement precedent without guaranteeing the outcome of each project.

evidence.note: The 15-inch/42 funding model applied to earlier development stages in other projects.

segments.summary: The scenario applies the funding approach used for the 15-inch/42 gun to other naval projects at an earlier stage.

segments.title: Was the Royal Navy already pursuing radical technology?
segments.body: The Royal Navy was already pressing for technical advances. Much of the development risk nevertheless rested with firms competing for its business. The proposed change puts public money into that process earlier. It changes who pays for experimental work and when the navy becomes directly involved.

evidence.note: Existing naval innovation relied on competing firms to finance development, while the scenario brings Admiralty funding forward.

segments.summary: The navy encouraged innovation, while competing firms often paid for early development themselves.
segments.question: Was the Royal Navy already operating like this between the mid-1800s and early 1900s?
segments.answerShort: It was pushing technology forward, but it often relied on industry and competition between firms to finance development; the scenario makes naval funding more proactive.

segments.title: Prizes for proven naval technology
segments.body: A discretionary fund could reward a demonstrated result. The Admiralty might publish a standard and pay the first builder to deliver a specified number of working 14-inch barrels that passed its test. This would make the payment a prize for success rather than a contribution to a firm's development costs as work proceeded. The outcome would depend on the competition's terms and on what each firm delivered, making the winning design impossible to assume in advance.

evidence.note: Discretionary funds could reward the first firm to deliver enough working barrels to a stated test standard.

segments.summary: The Admiralty could offer a prize for the first firm to deliver working guns that met a stated test standard.

segments.title: Earlier fire-control superstructures
segments.body: Longer-range gunnery could change the structures used for visual sighting. Pagoda-style masts might appear earlier and in navies beyond Japan. A Queen Anne's Mansions arrangement is another possibility raised for fire control. These remain alternative design ideas whose adoption would depend on how the wider research programme developed.

evidence.note: Possible earlier pagoda-style masts in navies beyond Japan.
Queen Anne's Mansions raised as another fire-control arrangement.

segments.summary: The need for better visual sighting could encourage earlier pagoda masts or Queen Anne's Mansions-style structures.

segments.title: How large could rangefinders become?
segments.body: Rangefinders have practical limits, but a triple 14-inch turret offers more room for a turret-mounted instrument. The larger mounting affects the ship's internal dimensions as well. In this reconstruction, Dreadnought would have a broader central core while remaining slightly narrower overall. The available space therefore depends on the mounting and hull arrangement, so no single maximum rangefinder length is proposed.

evidence.note: Larger turret space and a broader central core within a slightly narrower reconstructed Dreadnought.

segments.summary: Larger triple turrets create room for bigger rangefinders, even when the ship as a whole becomes slightly narrower.
segments.question: How large might naval rangefinders become in this scenario?
segments.answerShort: Their length has practical limits, but larger triple turrets provide more room; the ship's detailed arrangement determines what will fit.

segments.title: Could optics and radar keep pace with longer-range guns?
segments.body: Optical manufacturers would have reason to improve their products as guns reached farther. Vickers made sights, while firms such as Taylor Hobson supplied lenses that went into them. Better optical instruments would help a fleet use the range of its new guns. Radar faces more obstacles, making a working system before World War I doubtful in this scenario. Sustained incentives could nevertheless bring radar and radar-directed fire control forward, with the end of the war offered as a possibility.

evidence.note: Optical sights and lens manufacture, with strong doubt about radar before World War I and a speculative earlier wartime arrival.

segments.summary: Longer-range guns would encourage sight and lens development, while radar before World War I remains doubtful.
segments.question: What could the research programme achieve in optics for sighting and fire control?
segments.answerShort: It would encourage optical manufacturers to improve sights and lenses alongside the guns; radar before World War I remains doubtful, though sustained incentives could bring it forward.

segments.title: Does a long-range gun need better accuracy to be useful?
segments.body: A gun's ability to reach a distant target creates a reason to improve the means of hitting it. Greater reach directs further development effort towards accuracy. It does not make the weapon pointless while reliable hitting remains difficult.

evidence.note: Closing clarification that longer gun range encourages accuracy work.

segments.summary: Greater range creates an incentive to improve accuracy; uncertain hitting does not make the gun wholly pointless.
segments.question: Is there no point in a long-range gun if it cannot hit reliably?
segments.answerShort: Greater reach gives a navy reason to work on hitting at that distance; the gun still has value while that work continues.
